question: What does @RestController do in Spring Boot?
title: @RestController in Spring Boot — Annotation Explained
direct_answer: @RestController combines @Controller and @ResponseBody. It registers an MVC controller whose handler return values use response-body processing rather than view-name resolution. A compatible HttpMessageConverter writes the response; JSON via Jackson is common, but the annotation also supports text, XML, bytes, resources, and other configured representations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring's most common REST annotation and how it simplifies JSON API development compared to traditional @Controller.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding @ResponseBody to methods inside a @RestController class, which is redundant since @RestController already implies @ResponseBody for all methods.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @RestController is a meta-annotation (composed annotation) that internally combines @Controller and @ResponseBody, showing knowledge of Spring's annotation composition model.

sections.title: What @RestController Does
sections.content:
The class still uses the normal Spring MVC machinery: request mappings choose a method, argument resolvers bind inputs, validation can run, and exception resolvers handle failures. The only defining shortcut is class-wide response-body semantics.

Use @Controller for a class centered on rendered views, and @RestController for an API-centered class. A @Controller can still write selected bodies with @ResponseBody or ResponseEntity.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: It is a convenience meta-annotation: @Controller + @ResponseBody.
Return values are written to the body unless another return handler applies.
Content negotiation and converters decide the media type.
It does not itself serialize objects or require Jackson.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: When a method returns CustomerDto and JSON is negotiated, the Jackson message converter normally writes it as JSON. If it returns Resource for a file download, a resource converter writes the body. A String can become text. @RestController removes repeated @ResponseBody annotations; it does not mean every response has Content-Type application/json.

sections.title: @RestController at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|@RestController|~@Controller + @ResponseBody|one stereotype annotation|marks a REST web controller|since Spring 4
blue|Every method|~Returns data, not a view|object serialized to JSON|via Jackson converter|no ViewResolver
emerald|Use for|~REST APIs|DTOs, records, lists|consumed by JS/mobile|the modern default
rose|Trap|~Using @Controller for JSON|needs @ResponseBody per method|repetitive + error-prone|@RestController fixes it

sections.title: Basic @RestController Example
When to Use @RestController
sections.content:
Use **@RestController** when building REST APIs that return JSON or XML data instead of HTML pages. This is the standard choice for modern backend services consumed by frontend frameworks (React, Angular) or mobile apps. If you're building a **Spring Boot microservice** that exposes endpoints for data exchange, @RestController is your default annotation.

Use traditional **@Controller** only when you need server-side rendering with Thymeleaf or JSP templates. If your endpoints mix data and views—some return JSON, others return HTML—use @Controller and add @ResponseBody selectively to JSON-returning methods. For pure REST APIs serving SPAs or mobile clients, @RestController is the cleaner, more declarative choice.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Redundant @ResponseBody**: Freshers often add @ResponseBody to individual methods inside a @RestController class. This is unnecessary because @RestController already applies @ResponseBody to all methods. It's like wearing two jackets—the annotation is already there.
- **Mixing @Controller and @RestController**: Using @Controller for REST endpoints and manually adding @ResponseBody everywhere. This creates inconsistency in the codebase. Stick to @RestController for REST APIs to make intent clear.
- **Forgetting @RequestMapping**: Placing @RestController without a base @RequestMapping path means every method needs a full path, leading to duplication. Always define the base path at class level for cleaner code.

followup_questions: What is the difference between @Controller and @RestController?
What HTTP status code does @RestController return by default?
How do you return a custom HTTP status code from a @RestController method?

seo.metaTitle: @RestController in Spring Boot | Java Fresher Interview Guide
seo.metaDescription: Learn what @RestController does — @Controller + @ResponseBody composed annotation, JSON serialization with Jackson, and how it differs from @Controller.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: @RestController is two annotations in one — and understanding which two tells you exactly how it works.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: @RestController is a composed annotation that combines @Controller and @ResponseBody. @Controller registers the class as a Spring bean picked up by component scanning. @ResponseBody tells Spring to serialize every method's return value directly into the HTTP response body instead of treating it as a view name.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: Before Spring 4, you had to add @ResponseBody to every single method in a REST controller. @RestController was introduced to eliminate that repetition. One annotation on the class, and all methods get the behavior.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: Default HTTP status: 200 OK for every method unless you override it.
JSON output: with Jackson on the classpath, return objects are serialized to JSON automatically.
No view resolution: return values go to MessageConverter, not ViewResolver.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: candidates miss: @RestController already includes @ResponseBody. Adding @ResponseBody explicitly on methods inside a @RestController class is redundant — it does nothing extra. Interviewers notice that.

speakable_v2.cap: Use ResponseEntity when you need custom headers or conditional status codes. For everything else, a plain return type with @RestController is cleaner.

question: What is the difference between @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, and @PatchMapping?
title: HTTP Method Annotations in Spring — GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH
direct_answer: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, and @PatchMapping are composed @RequestMapping annotations that restrict handler selection to the corresponding HTTP method. They do not enforce REST behavior. GET is defined as safe; PUT and DELETE are idempotent by HTTP semantics; POST is general processing; PATCH applies a partial modification document whose media type defines its rules.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of RESTful conventions and proper HTTP method semantics, which is fundamental to designing clean REST APIs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @PostMapping for all operations including updates, when @PutMapping or @PatchMapping is semantically correct for modifications.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the idempotency property: GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent (multiple identical requests produce the same result), while POST is not, which affects API design decisions.

sections.title: Spring's HTTP Method Mapping Annotations
sections.content:
Mappings can also restrict path, params, headers, consumes, and produces. If two mappings remain equally specific, startup or request mapping can fail with ambiguity.

PATCH is not automatically JSON merge. application/json-patch+json and application/merge-patch+json have different semantics, and an ordinary DTO-based patch needs explicit rules for omitted versus null fields.

**Example.** @GetMapping("/orders/{id}") reads an order, @PostMapping("/orders") creates one, @PutMapping replaces the chosen representation, @PatchMapping applies a partial change, and @DeleteMapping removes it. The service must still implement the matching semantics.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: GET retrieves a representation and must not be used for a requested state change.
POST submits data for processing and often creates a subordinate resource.
PUT creates/replaces the state at a known URI and is idempotent.
PATCH applies partial changes; validate the patch format and concurrency contract.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Spring will happily map a @GetMapping method that deletes data, but that violates HTTP safety and can be triggered by crawlers or caches. @PostMapping is not limited to creation. @PutMapping can create a resource at a client-known URI or replace it. @DeleteMapping can return different success statuses while remaining idempotent: repeating it should not create additional intended state changes.

sections.title: HTTP Verb Mapping Annotations
sections.content:
amber|@GetMapping|~Retrieve data|safe + idempotent|no request body|@PostMapping creates resources
blue|@PutMapping vs @PatchMapping|~Full vs partial update|PUT replaces the whole resource|PATCH updates some fields|both idempotent in spirit
emerald|@DeleteMapping|~Removes a resource|often returns 204|idempotent|maps to DELETE
rose|Trap|~Using GET to modify|GET must be read-only|breaks caching + REST|pick the verb by intent

sections.title: All Five HTTP Method Mappings
When to Use Each Method
sections.content:
Use **@GetMapping** for retrieving data without side effects—fetching a user profile, listing products, searching orders. GET requests should never modify data.

Use **@PostMapping** for creating new resources where each request generates a unique entity—submitting a new order, registering a user, uploading a file.

Use **@PutMapping** for full resource replacement where you send the complete updated object—updating all fields of a user profile, replacing an entire configuration.

Use **@PatchMapping** for partial updates where you send only changed fields—updating just a user's email, changing a product's price.

Use **@DeleteMapping** for removing resources—deleting a user account, removing a product from inventory. The critical decision is POST vs PUT vs PATCH for modifications: POST creates, PUT replaces everything, PATCH changes parts.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using POST for everything**: Freshers often use POST for all operations including updates because it works, but this violates REST conventions and breaks caching, idempotency expectations. Clients can't safely retry POST requests.
- **Confusing PUT and PATCH**: Using PUT when only updating one field sends unnecessary data and risks overwriting fields not included in the request. PUT expects the full object; PATCH expects only changes.
- **GET with request body**: Trying to send data in a GET request body. GET should only use query parameters and path variables; the body is typically ignored by servers.
- **Ignoring idempotency**: Not understanding that multiple identical PUT or DELETE requests should produce the same result, while POST creates duplicates. This affects retry logic and error handling in production.

followup_questions: What is idempotency and which HTTP methods are idempotent?
What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
What HTTP status code should a POST request return on success?

seo.metaDescription: Learn Spring HTTP method annotations — GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE semantics, idempotency, and correct response status codes for REST APIs.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: Five HTTP methods, five annotations — but the real question is which one matches the operation you're actually performing.

beats.label: optimising_for
beats.content: Each mapping annotation corresponds to an HTTP verb with a specific semantic meaning in REST. Picking the right one isn't just style — it signals intent to every developer and every HTTP client that sees your API.

beats.label: options
rows: Full replace — send the whole entity
Partial update — send only changed fields

beats.label: tradeoffs
beats.content: Idempotency is the key concept here. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent — calling them ten times has the same effect as calling them once. POST is not — ten POST calls create ten records. PATCH is technically not idempotent in the general case either.

beats.label: decision
beats.content: Use @PostMapping and return 201 Created for creates. Use @DeleteMapping and return 204 No Content when there's nothing to return. Use @PutMapping when the client sends a full replacement. Use @PatchMapping when they send only what changed.

beats.label: rethink_if
beats.content: sharp edge: Using @PostMapping for updates is a common fresher mistake. A POST that creates ten identical resources is correct REST. If you only want one resource to exist, you need PUT or PATCH.

speakable_v2.cap: All five annotations are shorthand for @RequestMapping with the method pre-set. You can always fall back to @RequestMapping if you need to match multiple HTTP methods.

question: How does Jackson serialize Java objects to JSON in Spring Boot?
title: Jackson JSON Serialization in Spring Boot — Auto-Configuration
direct_answer: When Jackson support and Spring MVC are configured, MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter can use the configured ObjectMapper to write a compatible return value as JSON. Spring selects that converter through response-body handling and content negotiation. It is an implementation detail to describe this as intercepting the method and directly calling writeValueAsString; converters commonly write to the response stream.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the internal serialization mechanism that converts Java objects to JSON in Spring REST APIs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not realizing Jackson uses getter methods by default for serialization—a field without a getter won't appear in the JSON output.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention useful Jackson annotations like @JsonProperty for custom field names, @JsonIgnore to exclude fields, or @JsonInclude to control null handling.

sections.title: How a Controller Return Value Becomes JSON
sections.content:
Serialization errors can occur after the controller method succeeds, for example because of an unsupported type or a getter that throws. Test the JSON contract rather than only testing the service result.

Use Jackson annotations or dedicated DTOs to define public fields, but avoid spreading persistence-specific lazy loading into serialization. Content-Type should be the media type actually written by the chosen converter.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Handler return-value processing chooses a converter after the controller returns.
ObjectMapper configuration controls properties, modules, naming, dates, and visibility.
Accept/produces and converter capability decide whether JSON is selected.
Lazy entities and bidirectional graphs should not be exposed blindly; map API DTOs deliberately.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Returning UserDto from a @RestController with an acceptable application/json response lets the Jackson converter serialize its properties. Boot can provide an ObjectMapper and register modules found under its conditions. A user-defined mapper or converter changes that setup. If the response is text/plaintext or a Resource, another converter can be selected instead.

sections.title: Jackson JSON Serialization
sections.content:
amber|ObjectMapper|~Jackson's engine|auto-configured by Boot|reads + writes JSON|the default serializer
blue|How|~MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter|intercepts the return value|ObjectMapper to JSON|written to response body
emerald|Customize|~@JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore|@JsonFormat for dates|or an ObjectMapper bean|control the output shape
rose|Trap|~No getters / fields|Jackson serializes nothing|records work out of the box|expose what you mean to

sections.title: Jackson Serialization Example
When Jackson Serialization Applies
sections.content:
Jackson serialization happens automatically in **@RestController** methods that return objects. Any return type—POJOs, records, collections like List or Map, even Spring's ResponseEntity wrapping an object—gets serialized. You don't explicitly call Jackson; Spring's HttpMessageConverter infrastructure triggers it when the client requests application slash json (via Accept header).

Use Jackson annotations when you need **custom serialization behavior**: at-JsonProperty to rename fields (map Java's userId to JSON's user_id), at-JsonIgnore to exclude sensitive fields like passwords, at-JsonInclude(Include.NON_NULL) to omit null fields for cleaner responses. For complex scenarios like custom date formats or bidirectional relationships, configure the **ObjectMapper bean** globally in a Configuration class. Jackson is the default for REST APIs, but if you need XML, Spring can use JAXB or Jackson's XML module instead.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Missing getters**: Freshers create POJOs with public fields but no getter methods. Jackson won't serialize those fields because it looks for getters by default. Always generate getters or use records (which have implicit getters).
- **Infinite recursion**: Bidirectional relationships like User has List of Orders and Order has User reference cause Jackson to loop infinitely. Fix with at-JsonIgnore on one side or at-JsonManagedReference and at-JsonBackReference.
- **Sensitive data leakage**: Returning entity objects directly from repositories without DTOs, exposing password hashes or internal IDs in JSON. Use dedicated response classes or at-JsonIgnore on sensitive fields.
- **Wrong date format**: Not configuring date serialization, leading to long timestamps instead of readable ISO-8601 strings. Records and modern Java time types handle this correctly, but older code with Date or custom types needs configuration.

What is @JsonProperty and when do you use it?
How do you handle circular references in JSON serialization?

seo.metaTitle: Jackson JSON Serialization in Spring Boot | Interview Guide
seo.metaDescription: Learn how Jackson serializes Java objects to JSON in Spring Boot — ObjectMapper, MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter, @JsonIgnore, @JsonProperty explained.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: Jackson is what actually turns your Java objects into JSON — and knowing how it works helps you fix serialization bugs fast.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: Jackson is Spring Boot's default JSON library. When your @RestController method returns a Java object, Spring passes it to MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter, which uses Jackson's ObjectMapper to convert it to JSON. Spring Boot auto-configures all of this when spring-boot-starter-web is on your classpath.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: By default, Jackson serializes fields that have public getters. If a field has no getter, it won't appear in the JSON output. This is why Lombok's @Getter or manually writing getters is important for DTO classes.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: @JsonIgnore: exclude a field entirely — typical use is hiding password fields.
@JsonProperty("user_name"): rename the field in the JSON output.
@JsonInclude(NON_NULL): skip fields that are null, keeping the JSON clean.
@JsonFormat(pattern="yyyy-MM-dd"): control how dates appear in JSON.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: production trap: Bidirectional JPA relationships like User has many Orders, Order has a User cause infinite recursion during serialization. Jackson follows each reference back and forth until a stack overflow. Use @JsonManagedReference and @JsonBackReference, or better yet, use DTOs instead of serializing entities directly.

speakable_v2.cap: Define an ObjectMapper bean in your configuration class to set global Jackson behavior — things like date format, null handling, or pretty printing.

How do you handle circular references in JSON serialization?

question: What is @ResponseStatus in Spring MVC?
title: @ResponseStatus in Spring — Custom HTTP Status Codes
direct_answer: @ResponseStatus associates a fixed HTTP status and optional reason with a controller method or exception type. A method annotation suits a response whose success status is constant. An exception annotation can be resolved when that exception reaches Spring MVC's exception handling. It does not turn failures thrown anywhere in the application, such as a swallowed scheduler exception, into an HTTP response.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of HTTP status code control mechanisms in Spring REST and how to signal different outcomes to API clients.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always using ResponseEntity for status code control when @ResponseStatus provides a simpler, more declarative approach for common cases.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate @ResponseStatus on exception classes to show automatic exception-to-HTTP-status mapping, which is a cleaner pattern than manually catching exceptions in every controller method.

sections.title: Using @ResponseStatus for Fixed Status Mapping
sections.content: ResponseEntity's return-value handling can supply its own status and headers, so mixing it with @ResponseStatus on the same method is confusing and unnecessary. Exception annotations also couple a domain exception to HTTP; shared libraries may prefer advice that maps the same exception differently at each boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Use a method annotation for one fixed response status.
Use ResponseEntity when status, headers, or body vary at runtime.
Use @ExceptionHandler/advice when the error body needs a consistent contract.
Avoid the reason attribute for REST bodies because it can use servlet sendError behavior.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For example, @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT) on a successful void delete method fixes its normal status at 204. An OrderNotFoundException annotated NOT_FOUND can become 404 when it escapes a controller request. If one method returns either 200 with a body or 404, ResponseEntity or exception handling expresses that branch more clearly.

sections.title: @ResponseStatus at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|@ResponseStatus|~Sets a fixed HTTP status|on a method or exception|declarative, compile-time|e.g. 201 Created
blue|On a method|~Overrides the default 200|same status every call|good for create = 201|no ResponseEntity needed
emerald|On an exception|~Maps exception to status|ResourceNotFound to 404|thrown anywhere|clean error codes
rose|Trap|~Status must vary|@ResponseStatus is fixed|use ResponseEntity instead|for runtime decisions

sections.title: @ResponseStatus on Methods and Exceptions
When to Use @ResponseStatus
sections.content:
Use **@ResponseStatus on methods** for common fixed status codes: 201 Created for POST endpoints that create resources, 204 No Content for DELETE endpoints that return nothing, 202 Accepted for async operations. This is cleaner than wrapping every return value in ResponseEntity when you don't need dynamic status control.

Use **@ResponseStatus on exception classes** to centralize error-to-status-code mapping: mark ResourceNotFoundException with 404, ValidationException with 400, UnauthorizedException with 401. This eliminates boilerplate try-catch blocks in controllers.

Use **ResponseEntity** instead when you need dynamic status codes based on business logic (return 200 if found, 404 if not) or must set custom headers like Location or Cache-Control. For simple CRUD APIs, at-ResponseStatus on methods and exceptions keeps code clean. For complex scenarios with conditional responses, ResponseEntity gives necessary flexibility.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Overusing ResponseEntity**: Freshers learn ResponseEntity first and use it everywhere, even when at-ResponseStatus would be simpler. If the status code is always 201 for a POST method, at-ResponseStatus is more readable than ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(order).
- **Forgetting on exceptions**: Not annotating custom exceptions, then manually catching them in every controller to return the right status. Mark the exception class once with at-ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) and Spring handles it globally.
- **Mixing approaches inconsistently**: Using at-ResponseStatus on some methods and ResponseEntity on others for the same status code, creating inconsistent patterns. Pick one approach per use case.
- **Not understanding precedence**: If both at-ResponseStatus and ResponseEntity are present, ResponseEntity wins. The annotation is ignored when you explicitly return ResponseEntity, which can confuse debugging.

followup_questions: What is the difference between @ResponseStatus and ResponseEntity?
How do you return 201 Created from a POST endpoint?
When would you use @ResponseStatus on an exception class vs @ExceptionHandler?

seo.metaTitle: @ResponseStatus in Spring MVC | Java Fresher Interview Guide
seo.metaDescription: Learn @ResponseStatus in Spring MVC — setting HTTP status codes on methods and exception classes, 201 Created, 204 No Content, difference from ResponseEntity.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: @ResponseStatus is the simple path to custom HTTP status codes — ResponseEntity is the powerful one. Pick based on what you need.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: @ResponseStatus is an annotation you put on a method or an exception class to declare what HTTP status code it produces. It's declarative and static — you set it once and it always applies.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: ResponseEntity is a return type that gives you full programmatic control — status code, headers, and body all in one object. You build it in the method body, so the status can depend on runtime logic.

beats.label: differences
content: @ResponseStatus on a method: always returns that status code, no conditions.
@ResponseStatus on an exception class: any time that exception propagates out of a controller, Spring returns that status automatically — no @ExceptionHandler needed.
ResponseEntity: build the response programmatically — status, headers, and body all customizable at runtime.

beats.label: when_to_pick
beats.content: Use @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED) on a simple POST method when you always return 201. Use ResponseEntity when you need to conditionally return 200 or 404, or add Location headers. Use @ResponseStatus on a custom exception class as a simple mapping without writing an @ExceptionHandler.

beats.label: tiny_example
beats.content: non-obvious: @ResponseStatus has a reason attribute that sets the response body message. But Spring wraps it in the standard error response format — you don't get full control over the body. For a custom error body shape, use @ExceptionHandler with ResponseEntity.

speakable_v2.cap: For basic status code control, @ResponseStatus is cleaner. For any runtime logic, custom headers, or precise error body shape, use ResponseEntity.

question: What is @RequestMapping at class level vs method level in Spring?
title: @RequestMapping at Class vs Method Level — URL Composition
direct_answer: Class-level @RequestMapping sets a base URL prefix that applies to all methods in the controller. Method-level annotations (@GetMapping, @PostMapping, etc.) add sub-paths to this base. Spring concatenates them: a class-level /api/users plus a method-level /{id} creates the full endpoint /api/users/{id}, avoiding path duplication.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Spring MVC URL structuring and how to organize REST endpoints cleanly using hierarchical path composition.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating the full base path in every method mapping instead of extracting it to class level, leading to duplication and harder maintenance.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that @RequestMapping can map multiple paths in an array and that class-level mappings can also specify common headers, params, or produces/consumes constraints.

sections.title: Hierarchical Path Composition in Spring MVC
sections.content:
**@RequestMapping** at the class level acts as a **base path prefix** for all handler methods in that controller, while method-level annotations define sub-paths relative to that base. Spring's **DispatcherServlet** concatenates these paths when registering endpoints. If your controller handles all user-related operations, you put **@RequestMapping("/api/users")** at class level, then each method adds its specific path like **@GetMapping("/{id}")** or **@PostMapping**. The final URLs become /api/users/{id} and /api/users. This **hierarchical composition** eliminates duplication and makes refactoring easier—change the base path once instead of in twenty methods.

Think of it like a file system: the class is the folder (/api/users) and methods are files inside it (/{id}, /search). You can even apply **common constraints** at class level like produces = "application/json" or headers = "X-API-Version=1", and they inherit to all methods unless overridden. This design follows the **DRY principle** (Don't Repeat Yourself) and keeps your REST API structure clean and maintainable.

sections.title: @RequestMapping: Class vs Method
sections.content:
amber|Class level|~Base URL prefix|@RequestMapping("/api/users")|shared by all methods|sets the namespace
blue|Method level|~Sub-path + HTTP verb|@GetMapping("/{id}")|@PostMapping with no path|refines the route
emerald|Final URL|~Prefix + sub-path|/api/users + /{id}|= /api/users/{id}|Spring concatenates them
rose|Trap|~Leading-slash mismatch|double or missing slashes|keep one convention|test the resolved path

sections.title: Class-Level and Method-Level Path Composition
When to Use Class-Level Mapping
sections.content:
Use **class-level @RequestMapping** whenever your controller manages a single resource type like users, orders, or products. This groups all related operations under one base path following REST conventions.

Apply it when you have **multiple CRUD methods** (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) that share the same path prefix—extracting /api/users to class level means you never type it again in methods.

Use it to enforce **common constraints** across all endpoints: set produces = "application/json" at class level so every method returns JSON by default. For **versioned APIs**, put the version in the class-level path like @RequestMapping("/api/v2/users") so upgrading to v3 requires changing one line.

Avoid class-level mapping for **utility controllers** with unrelated methods like /health, /metrics, /export—those should use full paths at method level since they don't share a logical base.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Repeating Base Paths**: Learners write @GetMapping("/api/users/{id}") on every method instead of extracting /api/users to class level, violating DRY and making refactoring painful when paths change.
- **Forgetting Slash Rules**: Mixing /api/users (trailing slash absent) at class level with /{id} (leading slash present) at method level works, but inconsistency causes confusion. Spring normalizes slashes, but be consistent.
- **Overriding Accidentally**: Adding @RequestMapping at method level instead of @GetMapping completely replaces the HTTP method constraint, so your endpoint accepts ALL methods (GET, POST, DELETE) unless you specify method = RequestMethod.GET. Always use the specific annotations like @GetMapping at method level.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Class-Level @RequestMapping**: Sets a base URL prefix that applies to all handler methods in the controller, acting as a shared path segment
**Method-Level Annotations**: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, etc. add sub-paths to the class-level base; Spring concatenates them into the full endpoint URL
**Path Composition**: A class-level /api/users combined with method-level /{id} creates the final endpoint /api/users/{id}, eliminating duplication
**Multiple Paths**: Use an array like @GetMapping({"/search", "/find"}) to map one method to multiple URLs, both inheriting the class-level base path
**Common Constraints**: Class-level @RequestMapping can specify produces, consumes, headers, or params that all methods inherit unless explicitly overridden

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: When you put @RequestMapping at the class level, it sets a base URL prefix for all methods in that controller. Then your method-level annotations like @GetMapping or @PostMapping add sub-paths to that base. Spring concatenates them together to build the full endpoint. For example, if you have @RequestMapping with "/api/users" on the class, and @GetMapping with "/{id}" on a method, Spring combines them into /api/users/{id}. This hierarchical approach eliminates duplication. Instead of writing /api/users twenty times in every method, you write it once at class level. It makes refactoring way easier—if you need to change the base path to /v2/users, you edit one line instead of hunting through every method. A cool detail is that class-level @RequestMapping can also set common constraints like produces equals "application/json" or specific headers, and all methods inherit those settings unless they override them. A common mistake is repeating the full base path in every method mapping. That violates the DRY principle and creates maintenance headaches. Another gotcha is using @RequestMapping at method level instead of @GetMapping. That removes the HTTP method restriction, so your endpoint accidentally accepts all methods unless you specify method equals RequestMethod dot GET explicitly. Always use the specific annotations at method level.

seo.metaDescription: Learn how class-level and method-level @RequestMapping compose URLs in Spring MVC — base path, URL concatenation, API versioning pattern.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: Class-level @RequestMapping is what keeps your controller methods clean — you declare the base path once, and every method inherits it.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: @RequestMapping at the class level sets a base URL prefix for every method in that controller. Method-level @GetMapping and @PostMapping annotations then specify sub-paths relative to that base. Spring concatenates them to form the complete URL.

beats.label: example
beats.content: A class mapped to /api/v1/users with a method mapped to /{id} produces GET /api/v1/users/{id}. Spring handles the slash joining automatically. You don't need to repeat the base in every method.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: This pattern also enables clean API versioning. Put the version number in the class-level path. All methods in that controller automatically include it. When you need a v2, create a new controller class with a v2 base path.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: non-obvious: @RequestMapping can accept an array of paths — both /users and /people can point to the same controller class. This is rarely needed but valid. The same applies at the method level.

speakable_v2.cap: Without a class-level mapping, each method's path is an absolute URL from the root. With one, method paths are relative to it — cleaner and easier to refactor.

question: What is @CrossOrigin in Spring Boot and what does CORS mean?
title: @CrossOrigin in Spring Boot — CORS Configuration for REST APIs
direct_answer: CORS is a browser-enforced protocol that allows a server to grant selected cross-origin script requests that the same-origin policy would otherwise restrict. @CrossOrigin adds CORS policy metadata to a controller or method; Spring then writes the appropriate headers and handles preflight requests. CORS does not authenticate a caller and does not block non-browser clients.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of the CORS security issue that affects every frontend-backend integration where the API and web app are on different domains.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting allowedOrigins to wildcard asterisk in production, which disables CORS protection entirely and creates a security vulnerability.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the global CORS configuration approach using WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings() as a cleaner alternative to annotating every controller with @CrossOrigin.

sections.title: CORS and @CrossOrigin
sections.content:
Simple cross-origin requests may be sent directly and checked against the response header. Other requests first send an OPTIONS preflight with the intended method and headers. The browser sends the real request only if the response policy allows it.

Credentials change the rules: a wildcard origin cannot be used as a credentialed allow-origin response. Configure exact trusted origins, allowed methods, headers, and credential behavior, and coordinate the policy with Spring Security so preflight requests are not rejected before CORS processing.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: The browser enforces the same-origin policy; the server opts origins into cross-origin access.
An origin is scheme + host + port, not merely a domain name.
Preflight OPTIONS checks methods and headers for some requests.
Use a narrow global or controller policy; do not combine wildcard origins with credentials carelessly.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A frontend at https://app.example can call https://api.example only when the API's CORS response permits that origin. @CrossOrigin(origins = "https://app.example") can express that for a controller, while WebMvcConfigurer or Spring Security configuration is usually clearer for an application-wide policy. A curl request can still reach the API without CORS because CORS is a browser reading restriction, not a firewall or authorization system.

sections.title: @CrossOrigin and CORS
sections.content:
amber|CORS|~Browser security rule|blocks cross-origin JS calls|enforced by the browser|not the server alone
blue|@CrossOrigin|~Allows specific origins|on a method or class|sets Access-Control headers|Spring handles preflight
emerald|Preflight|~OPTIONS request first|browser asks permission|server replies allowed|then real request runs
rose|Trap|~allowedOrigins = "*" with credentials|browser rejects it|name explicit origins|tighten in production

sections.title: Using @CrossOrigin in a REST Controller
When to Enable CORS
sections.content: Use **@CrossOrigin** when your frontend and backend run on different domains or ports during development (localhost:3000 calling localhost:8080) or in production (app.example.com calling api.example.com). Enable it for **public APIs** that third-party websites should access, like a weather service API. You also need it for **mobile app backends** if your app uses a WebView to display content that calls your API. However, if your Spring Boot app serves both the frontend and API from the same domain using Thymeleaf or static resources, CORS isn't needed because it's same-origin. For **internal microservices** behind an API gateway, disable CORS on backend services and configure it only on the gateway facing browsers.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Wildcard in Production**: Using @CrossOrigin(origins = "*") disables CORS protection entirely, allowing any website to call your API and potentially steal user data through their browser. Use specific domains instead.
- **Forgetting Credentials**: When your frontend sends cookies or Authorization headers, you must set @CrossOrigin(allowCredentials = "true") AND specify exact origins (not wildcard), otherwise the browser blocks the request.
- **Annotating Every Method**: Freshers annotate every @GetMapping individually instead of putting @CrossOrigin once at class level, creating duplication. Use class-level for shared origins and method-level only for exceptions.

seo.metaTitle: @CrossOrigin and CORS in Spring Boot | Java Fresher Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn CORS and @CrossOrigin in Spring Boot — what CORS is, @CrossOrigin annotation, global WebMvcConfigurer CORS config, and Spring Security CORS.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: CORS errors in the browser are one of the most common shocks when you first connect a React frontend to a Spring Boot API.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: CORS stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. It's a browser security policy that blocks JavaScript on one origin from calling an API on a different origin. An origin is the combination of protocol, domain, and port — so localhost:3000 and localhost:8080 are different origins even though they're on the same machine.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: The browser enforces CORS to prevent malicious sites from making authenticated API calls on your behalf. It's not a Spring limitation — it's enforced by every browser. The server has to explicitly opt in to cross-origin requests by sending CORS response headers.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: @CrossOrigin on a controller: adds CORS headers for all methods in that class.
WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings: global CORS config applied to all endpoints — the cleaner production approach.
Preflight request: before a POST or PUT, the browser sends an OPTIONS request to check if cross-origin is allowed. Spring handles this automatically.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: sharp edge: allowedOrigins('*') allows every domain and is fine in development. But you can't combine it with allowCredentials(true) — that combination is rejected by the browser's CORS spec. In production, list your specific frontend domains explicitly.

speakable_v2.cap: If you add Spring Security later, configure CORS there too — Security processes requests before Spring MVC and can block preflight OPTIONS requests before your CORS config runs.
